Babylon's capture (verses 1–10)

Babylon lay in a flat country with abundant water.

Isaiah repeatedly predicted its destruction, which Henry also sees as a picture of the downfall of the great enemy of the New Testament church foretold in Revelation.

For oppressed captives, the news of Babylon's ruin would bring relief.

For proud oppressors, it would bring distress.

Let this teach us not to rely on empty amusement and bodily pleasure, because we do not know how suddenly laughter may end in grief.

Isaiah raises the alarm as Babylon is threatened by Cyrus.

The images of a donkey and a camel appear to Henry to represent the Medes and Persians.

Babylon's idols would be unable to protect the city; instead, they would themselves be broken.

Genuine believers are like grain on God's threshing floor.

Hypocrites resemble the chaff and straw mixed among the wheat until the harvest separates them.

God's grain should expect to be threshed by suffering and persecution.

Israel endured such afflictions, yet even in them the Lord still called the people his own.

Whatever happens to the church in the past, present or future, look to God.

He has the power to do anything for his church and the grace to do everything that serves her true good.

The watchman's message to Edom (verses 11 and 12)

God's prophets and ministers are like watchmen.

In peaceful times they guard the city to see that all is well.

In times of war they look for approaching danger and warn the people.

After long spiritual sleep, it is time to wake up and work.

Our journey is long and our duties many.

The question about the night asks whether dawn and relief are approaching.

Yet many people ask God's watchmen questions only out of curiosity, demanding difficult predictions or obscure prophecies explained.

They fail to inquire about their own souls, salvation and daily duty.

The prophet's reply points to morning followed by night.

Periods of light, health, youth or prosperity may be followed by illness, old age and adversity.

Use the present morning well to prepare for the night to come.

The call is urgent: Inquire. Return. Come.

There is no time for idle delay.

Those who return to God discover how much good work remains and how little time they have to accomplish it.

The danger awaiting Arabia (verses 13–17)

The peoples of Arabia lived in tents and kept flocks and herds.

An invading army would threaten them and make them vulnerable.

None of us knows what severe distress may arrive before death.

People who now eat abundantly may later lack even necessary bread.

Neither the ability of expert archers nor the courage of strong soldiers can protect a nation from God's judgments.

What a poor kind of glory can vanish so quickly!

The Lord has spoken, and none of his words will fail.

The Strength of Israel cannot lie.

Those who possess riches and glory beyond an invader's reach are truly blessed.

Every other form of prosperity is passing away.
classic_reading:
[Isa.21.1-Isa.21.10]
Chapter 21
The taking of Babylon. ( [Isa.21.1-Isa.21.10] Is. 21:1-10) Of the Edomites. ( [Isa.21.11] Is. 21:11, [Isa.21.12] 12) Of the Arabs. ( [Isa.21.13-Isa.21.17] Is. 21:13-17)
Verses 1-10 Babylon was a flat country, abundantly watered. The destruction of Babylon, so often prophesied of by Isaiah, was typical of the destruction of the great foe of the New Testament church, foretold in the Revelation. To the poor oppressed captives it would be welcome news; to the proud oppressors it would be grievous. Let this check vain mirth and sensual pleasures, that we know not in what heaviness the mirth may end. Here is the alarm given to Babylon, when forced by Cyrus. An ass and a camel seem to be the symbols of the Medes and Persians. Babylon's idols shall be so far from protecting her, that they shall be broken down. True believers are the corn of God's floor; hypocrites are but as chaff and straw, with which the wheat is now mixed, but from which it shall be separated. The corn of God's floor must expect to be threshed by afflictions and persecutions. God's Israel of old was afflicted. Even then God owns it is his still. In all events concerning the church, past, present, and to come, we must look to God, who has power to do any thing for his church, and grace to do every thing that is for her good.
[Isa.21.11-Isa.21.12]
Verse 11 ,12 God's prophets and ministers are as watchmen in the city in a time of peace, to see that all is safe. As watchmen in the camp in time of war, to warn of the motions of the enemy. After a long sleep in sin and security, it is time to rise, to awake out of sleep. We have a great deal of work to do, a long journey to go; it is time to be stirring. After a long dark night is there any hope of the day dawning? What tidings of the night? What happens to-night? We must never be secure. But many make curious inquiries of the watchmen. They would willingly have nice questions solved, or difficult prophecies interpreted; but they do not seek into the state of their own souls, about the way of salvation, and the path of duty. The watchman answers by way of prophecy. There comes first a morning of light, and peace, and opportunity; but afterward comes a night of trouble and calamity. If there be a morning of youth and health, there will come a night of sickness and old age; if a morning of prosperity in the family, in the public, yet we must look for changes. It is our wisdom to improve the present morning, in preparation for the night that is coming after it. Inquire, return, come. We are urged to do it quickly, for there is no time to trifle. Those that return and come to God, will find they have a great deal of work to do, and but little time to do it in.
[Isa.21.13-Isa.21.17]
Verses 13-17 The Arabians lived in tents, and kept cattle. A destroying army shall be brought upon them, and make them an easy prey. We know not what straits we may be brought into before we die. Those may know the want of necessary food who now eat bread to the full. Neither the skill of archers, nor the courage of mighty men, can protect from the judgments of God. That is poor glory, which will thus quickly come to nothing. Thus hath the Lord said to me; and no word of his shall fall to the ground. We may be sure the Strength of Israel will not lie. Happy are those only whose riches and glory are out of the reach of invaders; all other prosperity will speedily pass away.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe siege and taking of Jerusalem.1–7The wicked conduct of its inhabitants.8–14The displacing of Shebna, and the promotion of Eliakim, applied to the Messiah.15–25
Jerusalem's terror and suffering (verses 1–7)

Why was Jerusalem overwhelmed with fear?

Some of the dead were not killed by swords but by famine; others may have died from terror or become helpless through discouragement.

The leaders fled but were overtaken.

God's servants who see approaching judgments and warn sinners about them feel genuine grief at the prospect.

Yet even the most dreadful horrors of a city captured by force are only a faint picture of the terrors of the final day of wrath.

Defensive preparations without faith (verses 8–14)

Judah's weakness became more obvious than ever.

The people showed both confidence in earthly strength and careless disregard for divine warning.

They strengthened fortifications and secured the city's water supply.

These were practical measures, but they acted without seeking God, honoring him or depending upon his blessing.

Every created resource becomes useful only as the Lord makes it useful.

We should thank him for each gift and use it to serve him.

The people were contemptuous of divine justice even as God corrected them.

His purpose was to humble them and call them to repentance.

Instead they pursued pleasure and acted as though judgment and eternity did not matter.

Henry sees practical unbelief in life after death as a root of the selfish security and sensuality that ruin so many people.

Such disbelief dishonors God and rejects his appointed remedy.

Whether it expresses itself through presumptuous confidence or through despair, it can lead people to willful destruction.

Shebna removed, Eliakim appointed (verses 15–25)

Isaiah's warning to Shebna exposed his pride, vanity and imagined security.

How empty is worldly greatness when death can so soon bring it to nothing!

What lasting difference does it make whether a person's body rests in an elaborate tomb or beneath ordinary grass?

Someone who uses power to drive other people about may justly find himself driven from his own position.

Eliakim would replace Shebna.

Those entrusted with authority should ask God for the grace to perform their responsibilities properly.

Eliakim's appointment also points beyond itself.

Jesus describes his own authority as Mediator through the key of David (Revelation 3:7).

He possesses complete authority over the kingdom of heaven and every affair belonging to it.

Human rulers should act as fathers to the people under their care.

It is more honorable to bring goodness to one's family through faith and service than to inherit famous names or titles.

Worldly prestige adds no true excellence to a person. It hangs upon someone like a decoration that can soon fall away.

Eliakim was compared with a nail fixed securely in a wall, on which his family could depend.

In Eastern houses, great nails or pegs were built into walls to hold household possessions.

Jesus Christ is the secure nail.

Whatever we entrust to him in faith cannot be finally lost.

He opens a door that no one can close and brings faithful believers, body and soul, into eternal glory.

But those who reject his salvation will discover that when he closes the door, no one can open it—whether they are excluded from heaven or confined under final judgment.
classic_reading:
[Isa.22.1-Isa.22.7]
Chapter 22
The siege and taking of Jerusalem. ( [Isa.22.1-Isa.22.7] Is. 22:1-7) The wicked conduct of its inhabitants. ( [Isa.22.8-Isa.22.14] Is. 22:8-14) The displacing of Shebna, and the promotion of Eliakim, applied to the Messiah. ( [Isa.22.15-Isa.22.25] Is. 22:15-25)
Verses 1-7 Why is Jerusalem in such terror? Her slain men are not slain with the sword, but with famine; or, slain with fear, disheartened. Their rulers fled, but were overtaken. The servants of God, who foresee and warn sinners of coming miseries, are affected by the prospect. But all the horrors of a city taken by storm, faintly shadow forth the terrors of the day of wrath.
[Isa.22.8-Isa.22.14]
Verses 8-14 The weakness of Judah now appeared more than ever. Now also they discovered their carnal confidence and their carnal security. They looked to the fortifications. They made sure of water for the city. But they were regardless of God in all these preparations. They did not care for his glory in what they did. They did not depend upon him for a blessing on their endeavours. For every creature is to us what God makes it to be; and we must bless him for it, and use it for him. There was great contempt of God's wrath and justice, in contending with them. God's design was to humble them, and bring them to repentance. They walked contrary to this. Actual disbelief of another life after this, is at the bottom of the carnal security and brutish sensuality, which are the sin, the shame, and ruin of so great a part of mankind. God was displeased at this. It is a sin against the remedy, and it is not likely they should ever repent of it. Whether this unbelief works by presumption or despair, it produces the same contempt of God, and is a token that a man will perish wilfully.
[Isa.22.15-Isa.22.25]
Verses 15-25 This message to Shebna is a reproof of his pride, vanity, and security; what vanity is all earthly grandeur, which death will so soon end! What will it avail, whether we are laid in a magnificent tomb, or covered with the green sod? Those who, when in power, turn and toss others, will be justly turned and tossed themselves. Eliakim should be put into Shebna's place. Those called to places of trust and power, should seek to God for grace to enable them to do their duty. Eliakim's advancement is described. Our Lord Jesus describes his own power as Mediator, Rev. 3:7, that he has the key of David. His power in the kingdom of heaven, and in ordering all the affairs of that kingdom, is absolute. Rulers should be fathers to those under their government; and the honour men bring unto their families, by their piety and usefulness, is more to be valued than what they derive from them by their names and titles. The glory of this world gives a man no real worth or excellence; it is but hung upon him, and it will soon drop from him. Eliakim was compared to a nail in a sure place; all his family are said to depend upon him. In eastern houses, rows of large spikes were built up in the walls. Upon these the moveables and utensils were hung. Our Lord Jesus is as a nail in a sure place. That soul cannot perish, nor that concern fall to the ground, which is by faith hung upon Christ. He will set before the believer an open door, which no man can shut, and bring both body and soul to eternal glory. But those who neglect so great salvation will find, that when he shutteth none can open, whether it be shutting out from heaven, or shutting up in hell for ever.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe overthrow of Tyre.1–14It is established again.15–18
Tyre's commercial greatness is brought low (verses 1–14)

Tyre had become a great marketplace for the nations. Its inhabitants were especially known for festivity and entertainment, and those pleasures made them reluctant to consider the warnings God sent through his servants.

Its merchants were as wealthy and honored as princes, and they lived with all the luxury of rulers.

Yet its splendor would not keep the city from destruction. When Tyre lay waste, the merchants would flee from it and seek shelter elsewhere.

Those who move away to escape a trouble that has unsettled them may discover that a different location cannot give them inward rest. When God's judgments pursue sinners, they will overtake them wherever they go.

How could such a wealthy and powerful city fall? Its destruction was from the Almighty.

God intended its fall to reveal the emptiness and uncertainty of earthly fame, magnificence and prosperity.

The ruin of Tyre warns every city and every person to beware of pride. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled.

The Lord had the power to bring this judgment himself; he chose to use the Chaldeans as his instruments.

Tyre's recovery and the right use of wealth (verses 15–18)

Tyre's ruin would not last forever. The Lord would eventually visit the city with mercy.

Yet when Tyre returned to commercial freedom, its people would once more practice the old arts through which they tempted others.

Love of worldly wealth is spiritual idolatry. Covetousness is also a form of idolatry.

The prophecy therefore teaches those who possess wealth to employ it in God's service.

When we remain in fellowship with God while pursuing our ordinary occupations, and do everything within our ability to advance the gospel, our goods and earnings become holy to the Lord, provided our true purpose is his glory.

Christians should undertake commercial work as God's servants, treating riches as possessions entrusted to them for which they must answer as his stewards.
classic_reading:
[Isa.23.1-Isa.23.14]
Chapter 23
The overthrow of Tyre. ( [Isa.23.1-Isa.23.14] Is. 23:1-14) It is established again. ( [Isa.23.15-Isa.23.18] Is. 23:15-18)
Verses 1-14 Tyre was the mart of the nations. She was noted for mirth and diversions; and this made her loth to consider the warnings God gave by his servants. Her merchants were princes, and lived like princes. Tyre being destroyed and laid waste, the merchants should abandon her. Flee to shift for thine own safety; but those that are uneasy in one place, will be so in another; for when God's judgments pursue sinners, they will overtake them. Whence shall all this trouble come? It is a destruction from the Almighty. God designed to convince men of the vanity and uncertainty of all earthly glory. Let the ruin of Tyre warn all places and persons to take heed of pride; for he who exalts himself shall be abased. God will do it, who has all power in his hand; but the Chaldeans shall be the instruments.
[Isa.23.15-Isa.23.18]
Verses 15-18 The desolations of Tyre were not to be for ever. The Lord will visit Tyre in mercy. But when set at liberty, she will use her old arts of temptation. The love of worldly wealth is spiritual idolatry; and covetousness is spiritual idolatry. This directs those that have wealth, to use it in the service of God. When we abide with God in our worldly callings, when we do all in our power to further the gospel, then our merchandise and hire are holiness to the Lord, if we look to his glory. Christians should carry on business as God's servants, and use riches as his stewards.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe desolation of the land.1–12A few shall be preserved.13–15God's kingdom advanced by his judgments.16–23
Sin brings desolation (verses 1–12)

People who place all their treasure and happiness in this world will eventually discover their poverty and misery.

We should apply Scripture's teaching about the vanity and frustration of everything under the sun to our own lives.

Sin has turned the earth upside down. The world is now very different for humanity from the dwelling God originally prepared.

Even at its finest, earthly beauty resembles a flower that fades while we are still holding it.

This world brings disappointment and tears. Our lives are short and full of trouble.

The curse of sin reaches every social rank and situation. God can empty and lay waste whatever people possess.

Human sin has polluted the earth, and the Lord's righteous judgment lays it desolate.

The pleasures of sinful indulgence will end in heaviness.

God has many ways to make wine and strong drink bitter to the people who depend upon them. Bodily illness, mental anguish and the destruction of a person's estate can transform pleasure into suffering.

Let us mourn for our sin and rejoice in God. No person or event can take away joy that is rooted in him.

A small faithful remnant remains (verses 13–15)

Even after the general destruction, a few faithful people will survive.

They will be scattered like the olives left after harvest, hidden among the leaves.

The Lord knows those who belong to him, although the world does not recognize them.

When worldly people's laughter stops, the saints can still rejoice, because the covenant of grace never fails. It is both the fountain of their comfort and the foundation of their hope.

Faith enables them to rejoice even under affliction and to encourage other sufferers to do the same.

Some may glorify the Lord in the fires of severe suffering; others may do so in low, dark and muddy valleys.

In every place, however remote, and amid every trial, however hot, let us continue thinking rightly of God's goodness.

If those trials cannot turn us from trusting him, we glorify the Lord in the fires.

God's final rule over judgment (verses 16–23)

Believers may be driven to the farthest regions of the earth and still be singing rather than sighing.

Yet Isaiah mourned the miseries he foresaw pouring across the earth like a torrent, and the small number of faithful people among its inhabitants.

Sin would abound, and evil would pursue those who practiced it.

Earthly security is deeply uncertain.

Worldly people imagine they occupy the earth as though it were a palace or impregnable castle. But their habitation is more like a temporary hut set up for one night.

The creation bears a heavy burden under sin and groans beneath it.

Ultimately the present order will fall, and new heavens and a new earth will appear, in which only righteousness dwells.

People who imagine their wealth or public office makes them unreachable will discover God's judgment against pride and cruelty.

We should not presume to announce the full meaning of God's dealings before the appointed time.

No one should feel secure merely because life is prosperous. Yet no sufferer need despair merely because circumstances are miserable.

God will receive glory through every judgment.

The mystery of his Providence has not yet been fully revealed.

The defeat of the Redeemer's enemies must make way for Christ's kingdom. Then the Sun of Righteousness will shine in full glory.

Let every unrepentant sinner consider the final outcome. The ungodly will sink beneath their transgressions and not rise again, while believers enjoy everlasting happiness.
classic_reading:
[Isa.24.1-Isa.24.12]
Chapter 24
The desolation of the land. ( [Isa.24.1-Isa.24.12] Is. 24:1-12) A few shall be preserved. ( [Isa.24.13-Isa.24.15] Is. 24:13-15) God's kingdom advanced by his judgments. ( [Isa.24.16-Isa.24.23] Is. 24:16-23)
Verses 1-12 All whose treasures and happiness are laid up on earth, will soon be brought to want and misery. It is good to apply to ourselves what the Scripture says of the vanity and vexation of spirit which attend all things here below. Sin has turned the earth upside down; the earth is become quite different to man, from what it was when God first made it to be his habitation. It is, at the best, like a flower, which withers in the hands of those that please themselves with it, and lay it in their bosoms. The world we live in is a world of disappointment, a vale of tears; the children of men in it are but of few days, and full of trouble, See the power of God's curse, how it makes all empty, and lays waste all ranks and conditions. Sin brings these calamities upon the earth; it is polluted by the sins of men, therefore it is made desolate by God's judgments. Carnal joy will soon be at end, and the end of it is heaviness. God has many ways to imbitter wine and strong drink to those who love them; distemper of body, anguish of mind, and the ruin of the estate, will make strong drink bitter, and the delights of sense tasteless. Let men learn to mourn for sin, and rejoice in God; then no man, no event, can take their joy from them.
[Isa.24.13-Isa.24.15]
Verses 13-15 There shall be a remnant preserved from the general ruin, and it shall be a devout and pious remnant. These few are dispersed; like the gleanings of the olive tree, hid under the leaves. The Lord knows those that are his; the world does not. When the mirth of carnal worldlings ceases, the joy of the saints is as lively as ever, because the covenant of grace, the fountain of their comforts, and the foundation of their hopes, never fails. Those who rejoice in the Lord can rejoice in tribulation, and by faith may triumph when all about them are in tears. They encourage their fellow-sufferers to do likewise, even those who are in the furnace of affliction. Or, in the valleys, low, dark, miry places. In every fire, even the hottest, in every place, even the remotest, let us keep up our good thoughts of God. If none of these trials move us, then we glorify the Lord in the fires.
[Isa.24.16-Isa.24.23]
Verses 16-23 Believers may be driven into the uttermost parts of the earth; but they are singing, not sighing. Here is terror to sinners; the prophet laments the miseries he saw breaking in like a torrent; and the small number of believers. He foresees that sin would abound. The meaning is plain, that evil pursues sinners. Unsteady, uncertain are all these things. Worldly men think to dwell in the earth as in a palace, as in a castle; but it shall be removed like a cottage, like a lodge put up for the night. It shall fall and not rise again; but there shall be new heavens and a new earth, in which shall dwell nothing but righteousness. Sin is a burden to the whole creation; it is a heavy burden, under which it groans now, and will sink at last. The high ones, that are puffed up with their grandeur, that think themselves out of the reach of danger, God will visit for their pride and cruelty. Let us judge nothing before the time, though some shall be visited. None in this world should be secure, though their condition be ever so prosperous; nor need any despair, though their condition be ever so deplorable. God will be glorified in all this. But the mystery of Providence is not yet finished. The ruin of the Redeemer's enemies must make way for his kingdom, and then the Sun of Righteousness will appear in full glory. Happy are those who take warning by the sentence against others; every impenitent sinner will sink under his transgression, and rise no more, while believers enjoy everlasting bliss.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA song of praise.1–5A declaration of the gospel blessings.6–8The destruction of the enemies of Christ's church.9–12
A song of praise for the Lord's protection (verses 1–5)

These words could celebrate the Jews' return from captivity. But Henry sees a greater fulfillment in praise for Christ's victories over our spiritual enemies and for the comfort he provides to all believers.

Genuine faith simply believes God's testimony and relies on the truth of his promises.

The Lord weakens proud people who consider themselves invincible, while strengthening those who are humble and look to him for support.

God shelters his people in every kind of weather.

He protects believers from arrogant oppressors. Their insults and threats are like the noise of strangers or the fierce sun at midday: intense for a moment, but where are they when the sun goes down?

The Lord has always been and will always remain a refuge for his distressed people.

He has prepared shelter for them, and he teaches them to run to it.

The gospel feast and victory over death (verses 6–8)

The New Testament often compares God's welcoming reception of repentant sinners to a feast.

The invitation extends to all peoples, Gentiles as well as Jews.

The gospel strengthens and cheers the hearts of those who have become conscious of their sin and mourn over it.

A veil covers the nations because humanity lives in spiritual darkness.

The Lord removes that veil through the light of the gospel and the Holy Spirit's power, enabling people to recognize and welcome divine truth.

Those long dead in trespasses and sins receive spiritual life.

Christ himself, in his resurrection, triumphs over death.

Sorrow will end. Those who mourn for sin will receive comfort; those who suffer for Christ will find consolation.

Yet the promise that God will wipe away every tear will be completely fulfilled only in the joys of heaven.

Hope in that future should help us resist excessive grief now, particularly the kind of weeping that prevents us from continuing to sow and do good.

Sometimes even in this life God removes the public shame borne by his people. But at the great day all their reproach will be removed.

Let us patiently endure sorrow and disgrace, knowing their time is short.

Waiting for the Redeemer and his final victory (verses 9–12)

People who longed for the promised Redeemer received the news of his coming with joy and praise.

Glorified believers will one day enter their Lord's joy with a triumphant song.

Waiting for Christ is never in vain. His mercy arrives with abundant compensation for every apparent delay.

The hands once extended upon the cross to accomplish salvation will finally be raised in judgment against those who persistently refuse him.

Henry reads Moab here as a figure representing all opponents of God's people. Their pride will be brought down through repeated judgments.

The defeat of Moab thus pictures Christ's final victory and the overthrow of Satan's strongholds.

Therefore, beloved brothers and sisters, remain steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the Lord's work, because your work in him is not wasted.
classic_reading:
[Isa.25.1-Isa.25.5]
Chapter 25
A song of praise. ( [Isa.25.1-Isa.25.5] Is. 25:1-5) A declaration of the gospel blessings. ( [Isa.25.6-Isa.25.8] Is. 25:6-8) The destruction of the enemies of Christ's church. ( [Isa.25.9-Isa.25.12] Is. 25:9-12)
Verses 1-5 However this might show the deliverance of the Jews out of captivity, it looked further, to the praises that should be offered up to God for Christ's victories over our spiritual enemies, and the comforts he has provided for all believers. True faith simply credits the Lord's testimony, and relies on his truth to perform his promises. As God weakens the strong who are proud and secure, so he strengthens the weak that are humble, and stay themselves upon him. God protects his people in all weathers. The Lord shelters those who trust in him from the insolence of oppressors. Their insolence is but the noise of strangers; it is like the heat of the sun scorching in the middle of the day; but where is it when the sun is set? The Lord ever was, and ever will be, the Refuge of distressed believers. Having provided them a shelter, he teaches them to flee unto it.
[Isa.25.6-Isa.25.8]
Verses 6-8 The kind reception of repentant sinners, is often in the New Testament likened to a feast. The guests invited are all people, Gentiles as well as Jews. There is that in the gospel which strengthens and makes glad the heart, and is fit for those who are under convictions of sin, and mourning for it. There is a veil spread over all nations, for all sat in darkness. But this veil the Lord will destroy, by the light of his gospel shining in the world, and the power of his Spirit opening men's eyes to receive it. He will raise those to spiritual life who were long dead in trespasses and sins. Christ will himself, in his resurrection, triumph over death. Grief shall be banished; there shall be perfect and endless joy. Those that mourn for sin shall be comforted. Those who suffer for Christ shall have consolations. But in the joys of heaven, and not short of them, will fully be brought to pass this saying, God shall wipe away all tears. The hope of this should now do away over-sorrow, all weeping that hinders sowing. Sometimes, in this world God takes away the reproach of his people from among men; however, it will be done fully at the great day. Let us patiently bear sorrow and shame now; both will be done away shortly.
[Isa.25.9-Isa.25.12]
Verses 9-12 With joy and praise will those entertain the glad tidings of the Redeemer, who looked for him; and with a triumphant song will glorified saints enter into the joy of their Lord. And it is not in vain to wait for him; for the mercy comes at last, with abundant recompence for the delay. The hands once stretched out upon the cross, to make way for our salvation, will at length be stretched forth to destroy all impenitent sinners. Moab is here put for all adversaries of God's people; they shall all be trodden down or threshed. God shall bring down the pride of the enemies by one humbling judgment after another. This destruction of Moab is typical of Christ's victory, and the pulling down of Satan's strong holds. Therefore, beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord; for your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Divine mercies encourage to confidence in God.1–4His judgments.5–11His people exhorted to wait upon Him.12–19Deliverance promised.20,21
God's unchanging covenant and perfect peace (verses 1–4)

The words “that day” seem to point, according to Henry, to the time when the New Testament Babylon will have been completely overthrown.

The unchanging promise and covenant of the Lord are the walls around his church.

The gates are open. Let sinners be encouraged to enter and belong to the Lord.

He keeps the person who trusts him in perfect peace: inward peace, outward peace, peace with God, peace of conscience, peace at every time and through every event.

Trust the Lord for such peace and for a lasting portion.

Everything sought from the world survives only briefly.

But those who trust God receive from him not merely comfort for the present, but strength that carries them toward everlasting happiness.

Let us acknowledge him in everything we do and depend upon him through every trial.

Waiting for God through his judgments (verses 5–11)

The righteous person's path is marked by steadiness, obedience and holy conduct.

God makes their path plain.

Their responsibility and comfort are to wait upon him and keep their desires directed toward him, even in the longest and darkest hours of distress.

We must never let suffering turn us away from God.

In a prolonged night of adversity, let our hearts desire him and pray for grace to remain faithful.

Religion without the heart has no real value, regardless of outward profession.

Even those who seek God early discover that he is already willing to receive them.

We must read to learn God's truth and will.

They pretend to address God while their thoughts wander among countless foolish things.

They substitute their own religious inventions for the worship he has commanded.

Many participate only to follow custom or pursue their personal advantage.

The former needs help and repentance; the latter is the hypocrisy God condemns here.

Those who quarrel with God or imagine they can conceal their intentions from him effectively accuse their Creator of ignorance.

The extraordinary change promised here may concern Judah's historical circumstances, but it also looks further ahead.

Through the gospel, a great harvest of souls would be gathered from the Gentiles into Christ's church.

People who genuinely rejoice in God even while troubled will eventually find greater cause for joy.

Meekness strengthens holy happiness.

Powerful enemies will be brought low, and mockers within the community will be judged.

But it is particularly unjust to make someone an offender for a single word.

But by despising God's word they destroyed the very foundations of their safety.

The nation would be shattered like a potter's vessel.

We should turn from our sinful paths and return to duty. That is the way of salvation.

True strength comes through quiet confidence in God and a mind resting upon him.

Instead, the people imagined themselves wiser than the Lord.

The plan they devised to rescue themselves became the very cause of their downfall.

Only a scattered few would escape as a warning to others.

Those who refuse to repent and seek happiness in God's favor and service merely hasten their ruin.

The Lord waits to be gracious to all who come to him through faith in Christ.

Happy are those who also wait upon him.

God's mercy and guidance for Zion (verses 19–26)

God's people will one day reach the heavenly Zion.

Then tears will be removed forever.

Even now, greater faithfulness in prayer would bring believers more comfort as well as more holiness.

A famine of God's word is worse than a famine of bread.

People face temptations both to the right and to the left.

Satan continually tries to draw us into side paths.

We are blessed when a faithful minister or friend, the warnings of conscience, or the Spirit's inward work corrects us when uncertain and restrains us before we go astray.

Through repentance, people come to hate the idols they once cherished.

The Lord accomplishes this daily in converting souls by his grace and teaching them to fear and love him.

Areas formerly lacking the means of grace will receive abundant instruction together with the Holy Spirit's influence.

The result should be comfort and joy for God's people.

The growing light represents increasing knowledge of divine truth.

This is the light brought by the gospel, announcing healing for the brokenhearted.

Assyria and all impenitent enemies judged (verses 27–33)

God restrains people from doing wrong.

A word is enough to direct his willing servants, while a bridle is needed to turn rebellious enemies toward their ruin.

The destruction of Sennacherib's army is also a picture of the future, everlasting judgment of those who persist in sin.

Tophet was a valley near Jerusalem.

Henry describes fires burning there to destroy offensive or dangerous things, and the hideous practice in which idolatrous Israelites made their children pass through the fire to Molech.

He treats this as an image of the certainty and severity of final punishment.

No oppressor can finally escape divine wrath.

Let sinners therefore flee to Christ and seek reconciliation with him.

Then they may be safe and blessed when the Almighty brings an end to everyone who continues in rebellion.
classic_reading:
[Isa.30.1-Isa.30.7]
Chapter 30
The Jews reproved for seeking aid from Egypt. ( [Isa.30.1-Isa.30.7] Is. 30:1-7) Judgements in consequence of their contempt of God's word. ( [Isa.30.8-Isa.30.18] Is. 30:8-18) God's mercies to his church. ( [Isa.30.19-Isa.30.26] Is. 30:19-26) The ruin of the Assyrian army, and of all God's enemies. ( [Isa.30.27-Isa.30.33] Is. 30:27-33)
Verses 1-7 It was often the fault and folly of the Jews, that when troubled by their neighbours on one side, they sought for succour from others, instead of looking up to God. Nor can we avoid the dreadful consequences of adding sin to sin, but by making the righteousness of Christ our refuge, and seeking for the sanctification of the Holy Spirit. Men have always been prone to lean to their own understandings, but this will end in their shame and misery. They would not trust in God. They took much pains to gain the Egyptians. The riches so spent turned to a bad account. See what dangers men run into who forsake God to follow their carnal confidences. The Creator is the Rock of ages, the creature a broken reed; we cannot expect too little from man, or too much from God. Our strength is to sit still, in humble dependence upon God and his goodness, and quiet submission to his will.
[Isa.30.8-Isa.30.18]
Verses 8-18 The Jews were the only professing people God then had in the world, yet many among them were rebellious. They had the light, but they loved darkness rather. The prophets checked them in their sinful pursuits, so that they could not proceed without fear; this they took amiss. But faithful ministers will not be driven from seeking to awaken sinners. God is the Holy One of Israel, and so they shall find him. They did not like to hear of his holy commandments and his hatred of sin; they desired that they might no more be reminded of these things. But as they despised the word of God, their sins undermined their safety. Their state would be dashed in pieces like a potter's vessel. Let us return from our evil ways, and settle in the way of duty; that is the way to be saved. Would we be strengthened, it must be in quietness and in confidence, keeping peace in our own minds, and relying upon God. They think themselves wiser than God; but the project by which they thought to save themselves was their ruin. Only here and there one shall escape, as a warning to others. If men will not repent, turn to God, and seek happiness in his favour and service, their desires will but hasten their ruin. Those who make God alone their confidence, will have comfort. God ever waits to be gracious to all that come to him by faith in Christ, and happy are those who wait for him.
[Isa.30.19-Isa.30.26]
Verses 19-26 God's people will soon arrive at the Zion above, and then they will weep no more for ever. Even now they would have more comfort, as well as holiness, if they were more constant in prayer. A famine of bread is not so great a judgment as a famine of the word of God. There are right-hand and left-hand errors; the tempter is busy courting us into by-paths. It is happy if, by the counsels of a faithful minister or friend, or the checks of conscience, and the strivings of God the Spirit, we are set right when doubting, and prevented from going wrong. They shall be cured of their idolatry. To all true penitents sin becomes very hateful. This is shown daily in the conversion of souls, by the power of Divine grace, to the fear and love of God. Abundant means of grace, with the influences of the Holy Spirit, would be extended to places destitute of them. The effect of this should be comfort and joy to the people of God. Light, that is, knowledge, shall increase. This is the light which the gospel brought into the world, and which proclaims healing to the broken-hearted.
[Isa.30.27-Isa.30.33]
Verses 27-33 God curbs and restrains from doing mischief. With a word he guides his people into the right way, but with a bridle he turns his enemies upon their own ruin. Here, in threatening the ruin of Sennacherib's army, the prophet points at the final and everlasting destruction of all impenitent sinners. Tophet was a valley near Jerusalem, where fires were continually burning to destroy things that were hurtful and offensive, and there the idolatrous Jews caused their children to pass through the fire to Moloch. This denotes the certainty of the destruction, as an awful emblem of the place of torment in the other world. No oppressor shall escape the Divine wrath. Let sinners then flee to Christ, seeking to be reconciled to Him, that they may be safe and happy, when destruction from the Almighty shall sweep away all the workers of iniquity.
